manuscript_title: The effects of Alcohol Dependence on the CSF

required_revisions.text: Resolve the BBB-disruption vs. collection-artifact question with a measured metric. Report per-sample hemoglobin and/or albumin concentration (CSF vs. serum ratio) and show whether it correlates with the Dep-specific protein detection pattern. If a blood-sparing collection method (e.g., Lourbopoulos 2025) is used, state this explicitly. Without this, the 'BBB breakdown' claim cannot stand as written.

Scale the causal and interpretive language to the evidence. Replace 'dichotomous/qualitative transition,' 'transition to alcohol dependence,' and 'BBB breakdown/dysfunction' with 'dependence-associated' and 'preliminary evidence consistent with' throughout the abstract, title, and discussion. State explicitly that the design cannot separate dependence from cumulative ethanol dose, route (vapor + i.p. injection vs. oral), and withdrawal stress, and that the dichotomy extends (rather than establishes) the authors' own companion transcriptomic work (Hashimoto 2025).

Resolve the immunoglobulin/immune-surveillance interpretation. Because the injected rat anti-IL-6R antibody (IGG2B, DILLISQNAK) was detected in every CSF sample, the KV5AB/LV1C/HVM02/03 detection patterns cannot be read as a clean measure of endogenous adaptive immunity. Either remove the 'loss of immune surveillance' claim or explicitly requalify it as entangled with the administered antibody and BBB permeability state.

Make all load-bearing artifacts accessible at submission. Make the GitHub repository public with a commit hash/tag (or deposit an archived copy, e.g., Zenodo DOI), and confirm the MassIVE accession is live, in the correct format (MSV0000xxxxx), and released at submission rather than 'upon publication.'

Add a sensitivity analysis for the detection threshold. Report the 140-vs-67 protein counts at ≥1 and ≥3 replicates and show that the biological interpretation survives threshold variation. Define the 'top 10' selection criterion for Figure 2.

Add a quantitative comparison of the 404 shared proteins (DIA provides quantitative peak areas). This is the analysis that could most strengthen or weaken every claim and serves as a partial control for the presence/absence framework.

Resolve the load-bearing citation questions. Confirm that ref 32 (Gaither 2025) actually reports BIP/GRP78 correlating with alcohol consumption grade in human liver biopsies (the cited title concerns drug-metabolizing enzymes/transporters) or correct the citation; and confirm that ProteomeXchange dataset PXD053568 (Lourbopoulos 2025) contains the Hb and keratin identifications claimed.

Add the missing methods details: animal age (weeks/months), a randomization/blinding statement, and a statement on MS precursor/fragment tolerances (or confirmation that DIA-NN handles these internally).

Report the sex composition of each group explicitly (the current sentence is ambiguous) and state whether any of the 140 Dep-specific proteins are driven predominantly by one sex; note the n=2-per-sex limitation in the Dep group.
Report total protein per CSF sample (or otherwise normalize detection for the 4-fold CSF volume range, 5–20 µL) to distinguish biological signal from sample-load technical variation.

minor_suggestions: State explicitly that the study extends a dichotomy already established in the same CIE-2BC model at the astrocyte transcriptome level (Hashimoto 2025), rather than presenting the dichotomy as this paper's own discovery.
Name a nearest-neighbor CSF proteomics study and state the delta over it, given that the individual markers (GFAP, MMP2, CHI3L1, UCHL1) are established biomarkers in other contexts.
Flag the single-peptide identification of the IL-6R antibody (DILLISQNAK) as a limitation in the main text, not merely in the supplement.
Add an RRID for the mouse strain and consider reporting confidence intervals for detection rates rather than (or in addition to) the post-hoc power analysis, which is circular.

Consider whether the anti-IL-6R antibody (150 kDa, present in CSF) itself alters BBB permeability, and integrate this into the BBB interpretation rather than treating it only as a methodological validation.

weaknesses.text: The central novelty claim — "alcohol exposure and alcohol dependence are dichotomous" — is a conceptual claim that outruns what this paper's evidence establishes, and it is partly preempted by the authors' own cited companion work. The dichotomy (dependence-specific neuroimmune activation vs. homeostatic response to moderate drinking) is already reported in the same CIE-2BC model at the astrocyte transcriptome level in Hashimoto et al. 2025, which the manuscript cites. The genuinely new delta here is the CSF proteomic evidence for that dichotomy, not the dichotomy itself. As framed ("This work provides novel protein-level evidence that..."), the claim is defensible, but the paper should state explicitly that it extends a dichotomy already established in this model rather than presenting the dichotomy as its own discovery. This is a SOFT positioning issue, not a HARD preemption — the CSF proteome comparison itself appears to be new.

The magnitude of the contribution is overstated relative to the evidence base for the "dichotomous" framing. The dichotomy rests on a qualitative detection-based analysis (present/absent at 1% FDR) in n=4–5 mice, with the authors' own power analysis conceding only 38% power for moderate effect sizes. A claim of qualitative dichotomy — that dependence produces a categorically different proteome rather than a quantitative escalation — is a strong inference from a design that cannot distinguish "not detected" from "below detection limit" and cannot resolve moderate effect sizes. The authors acknowledge this in the Limitations, which is to their credit, but the abstract and conclusions still assert the dichotomy more firmly than the evidence supports. The framing should be scaled to "preliminary evidence consistent with a qualitative shift," which is what the data actually support. (The statistical adequacy of this is rigor's call; I flag it only as a magnitude/positioning issue.)

Differentiation from the nearest competing work is thin. The manuscript cites human CSF studies in AUD (Azuar et al. 2021) and the mechanistic BBB literature but never names a nearest-neighbor CSF proteomics study and explains the delta over it. Given that the individual markers (GFAP, MMP2, CHI3L1, UCHL1) are all established biomarkers in other contexts, the paper's contribution is specifically the co-detection in CSF of dependent mice in this model — that should be stated as the differentiation, and a head-to-head against the closest human CSF proteomics work offered where feasible.

1. HARD — The causal attribution to "dependence" is confounded by the vapor procedure. The two groups differ in more than dependence status: Dep mice received ethanol vapor, ethanol+pyrazole injections, and repeated withdrawal cycles; Non-dep received only pyrazole and 2BC. The abstract's "dichotomous" framing and the conclusion's "transition to alcohol dependence" attribute the proteomic differences to the dependence state, but a design comparing vapor-exposed vs. non-vapor-exposed mice cannot isolate dependence from the vapor/withdrawal procedure itself. The alternative — that the differences reflect repeated ethanol exposure, withdrawal stress, or the injection regimen — is equally consistent with the data. This is partly methodology's call, but it bears directly on claim wording: "dependence-associated" is licensed; "dependence causes" or "transition to dependence" is not.

2. HARD — The immunoglobulin variable regions interpreted as "maintained adaptive immune surveillance" are confounded by the injected antibody. The authors themselves detected the rat anti-IL-6R antibody (IGG2B, peptide DILLISQNAK) in all CSF samples. The presence of immunoglobulin-derived peptides in CSF is therefore not a clean readout of endogenous adaptive immunity — it is entangled with the administered antibody and with BBB permeability state. Interpreting KV5AB/LV1C/HVM02/03 detection in Non-dep as evidence of intact immune surveillance, and their absence in Dep as "loss" of it, is not licensed. Differential antibody passage, clearance, or binding across groups would produce the same pattern. The authors flag the antibody's presence in a limitation but do not connect it to the immune-surveillance claim they make in the Abstract and Discussion.

3. SOFT — BBB disruption is inferred from protein identity, not measured. MMP2, BIP, VE-cadherin, and VCAM1 in CSF are consistent with barrier compromise, but no BBB permeability assay, tight junction quantification, or functional test is performed. MMP2 also participates in normal ECM turnover, and VE-cadherin could reflect endothelial shedding without frank barrier failure. The Abstract's "signatures of" is defensible; the Discussion's "BBB compromise" and "BBB dysfunction" are not. A functional assay (Evans blue or dextran permeability) or tight junction protein measurement would distinguish barrier breakdown from other release mechanisms.

questions: 1. Was there any cohort that did not receive anti-IL-6R whose CSF could be compared, to test whether the immunoglobulin signal and any group differences depend on the antibody?
2. Can the authors report the detection analysis restricted to proteins whose absence in the comparison group is not attributable to the injected antibody or to detection sensitivity limits?

3. What functional evidence (BBB permeability assay, tight junction staining) could be added to support the BBB disruption interpretation, and would the authors consider softening the Discussion's "BBB breakdown" language until such evidence exists?

weaknesses.text: The BBB-disruption claim is not distinguished from a collection artifact. The central claim — that Dep-specific vascular proteins (MMP2, VE-cadherin, VCAM1, LAMB2, fibulins) evidence in vivo BBB breakdown — rests on CSF drawn by cisterna magna puncture with a pulled pipette, a method that can introduce blood. The paper detects hemoglobin and keratins in Dep samples and dismisses them as trace contamination, but the same reasoning applies to the very proteins anchoring the BBB claim: if Dep vasculature is fragile (as the paper argues), the puncture could differentially contaminate Dep CSF with endothelial and blood proteins. The paper's own hypothesis predicts this confound and does not exclude it. Reporting a blood-marker ratio (hemoglobin or albumin normalized per sample) or using a blood-sparing collection method (e.g., the Lourbopoulos 2025 method the paper itself cites) would separate in vivo BBB leak from collection artifact.

The 'dichotomous/qualitative' framing outruns the detection-based evidence. The abstract's 'clear molecular transition' and the title's 'Evidence for Blood-Brain Barrier Dysfunction' state the dependence transition as qualitatively distinct, but the evidence is presence/absence at 1% FDR in n=4–5. A protein 'not detected' in DIA-MS is below the detection limit, not absent; the data support 'detectably different at this threshold,' not 'qualitatively distinct mechanisms.' The limitations acknowledge this ('minimum estimates'), but the abstract and title state it more strongly than the evidence allows.

The 'preserved protective mechanisms' reading of Non-dep proteins rests on unexamined technical variation. The interpretation of CALB1, SUMO2/3, TAGL3, and immunoglobulin regions as maintained protective mechanisms depends on detection asymmetry that could reflect sample load. CSF volumes ranged 5–20 µL (a 4-fold range); the paper does not report total protein per sample or normalize detection for it. If Non-dep samples carried higher protein load, more low-abundance proteins would be detected regardless of biology. Reporting total protein per sample or quantifying (not merely detecting) these proteins would distinguish a biological signal from a technical one.

questions: What is the sex composition of each group (Dep n=4, Non-dep n=5)? The methods sentence is ambiguous as written.
Which color corresponds to which group in Figure 1c — the text and legend disagree.
What was the total protein amount per CSF sample, and was detection normalized for it?

weaknesses.text: The central detection-rate comparisons are never tested statistically: no test is applied to any detection-rate difference (e.g., MMP2 at 4/4 Dep vs 0/5 Non-dep, GFAP at 3/4 vs 0/5, or the 140-vs-67 protein counts). A Fisher's exact test on the MMP2 table gives p = 0.0079 (two-sided); with ~600 proteins screened, even a single uncorrected comparison at this level is marginal, and none would survive any reasonable multiple-testing correction.

The 'Strong'/'Moderate' evidence classification in Tables 1–2 is an arbitrary detection-rate threshold, not a statistical result; the claim that 140 proteins are 'Dep-specific' is a descriptive observation, not a tested finding.

The detection threshold is arbitrary and the headline counts are threshold-dependent: the 140 vs 67 counts depend on the ≥2-replicate detection rule, and the asymmetry between the Dep criterion (≥3/4 = 75%) and Non-dep criterion (≥4/5 = 80%) means the two counts are not directly comparable.

No sensitivity analysis is reported — the counts at ≥1 replicate, or at ≥3 replicates, would likely change substantially, and the manuscript does not show that the biological interpretation survives threshold variation.
The 'top 10' selection for Figure 2 is undefined as a criterion.

Missing values are assumed to be 'below limit of detection' without verification: no spike-in controls, no technical replicates, no QC metrics (e.g., coefficient of variation across replicates, ion injection time distributions) support the MNAR assumption; in DIA-MS, missing values arise from ion suppression, co-elution, and technical variability as well as true absence.

The contamination question is not resolved for the specific claim it threatens: keratins (K2C5, K1C10, K2C1B) and hemoglobin are concentrated in the Dep group, and the cited methodological defense addresses whether these proteins can appear in clean CSF, not whether differential contamination occurred between groups; if BBB disruption makes CSF collection more difficult in Dep mice, the contamination signature would concentrate exactly where the manuscript reports it, and the 'BBB disruption' claim would be partly an artifact of the collection process.

Post-hoc power analysis is circular — it uses observed detection rates to claim the study was underpowered, which is always true for non-significant results; report confidence intervals for detection rates instead.
The 404 shared proteins are never compared quantitatively, despite DIA providing quantitative peak areas — a missed opportunity and a partial control for the presence/absence framework.
Enrichment analyses (EnrichR, STRING, KEGG) inherit the arbitrary detection threshold and are not corrected for the hundreds of pathways/terms tested.
Sex is a potential confound: PCA shows Non-dep separates by sex along PC2 but Dep does not — with n=2 per sex in the Dep group, this could be a power artifact rather than a biological signal.
The IL-6R antibody treatment is a confound for all comparisons; the claim that it 'did not ameliorate' Dep effects is unsupported by any data shown (no vehicle control is reported).
The single-peptide identification of the IL-6R antibody (DILLISQNAK) is weak evidence; the manuscript discloses this but should flag it as a limitation rather than presenting it as confirmation.

questions: What are the 140-vs-67 protein counts at detection thresholds of ≥1 and ≥3 replicates, and does the biological interpretation survive?
What is the per-sample hemoglobin concentration (or equivalent contamination metric), and does it correlate with the Dep-specific protein detection pattern?
Were any technical replicates or QC metrics (e.g., peptide CVs, injection time distributions) collected to support the MNAR assumption for missing values?
What is the sex breakdown of the 140 Dep-specific proteins — are any driven predominantly by one sex?

weaknesses.text: Dose and dependence are confounded; the qualitative-transition claim is not testable with this design (HARD). The Dep group differs from Non-dep in three variables simultaneously: total ethanol dose, route of administration (vapor + 1.75 g/kg i.p. injection vs oral 2BC), and the dependence phenotype. The manuscript frames its central question as whether dependence is a 'quantitative progression' or involves 'qualitatively distinct pathophysiological mechanisms,' but this design cannot separate those — the Dep group has both higher exposure and dependence. Any proteomic difference could reflect cumulative ethanol dose rather than the dependent state. A matched-exposure control (e.g., vapor-exposed mice that do not escalate drinking, or a group yoked for blood ethanol levels) would be required to attribute the signature to dependence per se. As written, the conclusion that the proteome reflects 'the transition to alcohol dependence' is not earned.

The BBB-disruption interpretation lacks a positive control for barrier integrity (HARD). Detection of MMP2, VE-cadherin, ACTA, and LAMB2 in Dep CSF is interpreted as BBB breakdown. Two alternative explanations are not excluded. First, blood contamination during cisterna magna collection: the manuscript's own data show hemoglobin and multiple keratins in the Dep-specific list, and the argument that 'MS detects trace amounts below ELISA limits' cuts both ways — trace blood contamination would produce exactly this pattern. Second, the anti-IL-6R antibody (150 kDa, administered i.p. to all mice) could itself alter BBB permeability or CSF composition; the finding that the antibody is present in CSF is evidence of permeability to large molecules that is not integrated into the BBB interpretation. A blood-borne tracer excluded from CSF in intact-barrier conditions (e.g., Evans blue, or a quantitative hemoglobin/albumin ratio) would distinguish true barrier breakdown from collection artefact or treatment effect. Without it, 'BBB disruption' is an interpretation, not a finding.

The 'protective mechanisms' interpretation of Non-dep-specific proteins outruns the evidence (SOFT–HARD). CALB1, SUMO2/3, and TAGL3 detected in Non-dep CSF are interpreted as 'maintained protective mechanisms' lost in dependence. These are presence/absence differences with no functional validation; the alternative — that these proteins are simply below the detection limit in Dep CSF, or present at different abundance for reasons unrelated to protection — is not addressed. The functional labels (calcium homeostasis, neuroprotection) are imported from the literature and applied to detection patterns. This is a reasonable hypothesis-generating observation, but the discussion presents it as a mechanism.
The analysis is entirely presence/absence; no quantitative comparison of shared proteins is reported, which would substantially strengthen (or weaken) every claim.
Sex is a potential confound that cannot be examined at n=4–5; the PCA shows Non-dep mice segregating by sex along PC2, which is acknowledged but not addressed.
All mice received anti-IL-6R antibody; the study cannot separate dependence effects from dependence-plus-IL6R-blockade effects, and this is underweighted relative to its importance.
The 'preferred' threshold (≥2/4 vs ≤1/5) is permissive, and no statistical test or multiple-testing correction is applied to detection-rate differences between groups.
The detection of the IL-6R antibody in CSF is presented as a methodological validation but is equally evidence relevant to BBB permeability; this internal inconsistency is not reconciled.

questions: Was any independent measure of BBB integrity collected (e.g., Evans blue extravasation, quantitative hemoglobin or albumin ratio in CSF vs serum)?
Were CSF samples screened for blood contamination (e.g., hemoglobin ELISA) prior to MS, and if so, what were the results?
Does the cohort include any vapor-exposed animals that did not escalate drinking, which could serve as a matched-exposure control?

weaknesses.text: The analysis code is inaccessible (HARD). The manuscript states: "All R scripts used for data analysis and figure generation can be found at the GitHub repository https://github.com/NataliePTurner/MouseCSF (private until published)." A private repository is not availability. These scripts generate the PCA, the heatmap, the enrichment analyses, and the power calculations — the core artifacts of the paper. An independent group cannot reproduce the figures or the protein-list generation from the raw data without them. This is precisely the "to be deposited upon publication with no accession" case the mandate flags as HARD for load-bearing artifacts. The fix: make the repo public with a commit hash/tag, or deposit an archived copy (e.g., Zenodo DOI) at submission.

The raw-data accession is unverifiable and in a non-standard format (HARD). The manuscript states the MS data are at MassIVE "with the dataset identifier C5GX4573B." MassIVE accessions follow the pattern MSV0000xxxxx; "C5GX4573B" does not match this format, and I could not verify it resolves. The raw MS data is the primary input to the entire analysis chain — if the accession is incorrect or the data is not yet released, the chain breaks at its first link. The fix: confirm the accession is live, in the correct format, and accessible without author intervention.

The processed-data-to-figure mapping cannot be confirmed. Supplementary file 1 (filtered quantitative data) is referenced, but I cannot inspect it, and the scripts that produce each figure are behind the private repo. The manuscript states which thresholds produce the heatmap and tables, but the full mapping (which script → which figure) is not verifiable. This is partly a consequence of weakness #1.

questions: Can the MassIVE accession be confirmed as live and in the correct format (MSV0000xxxxx), with the raw data released at submission rather than "upon publication"?
Will the GitHub repository be made public with a commit hash/tag, or deposited as an archived DOI, at submission?

weaknesses.text: The contamination defense rests on a citation I could not verify. The Limitations section rebuts the blood-contamination alternative to the Dep-specific protein list by citing Lourbopoulos 2025 and its ProteomeXchange dataset PXD053568 as containing Hb and keratin identifications despite undetectable Hb by ELISA. This is the entire citation-based answer to the alternative that the Dep-specific proteins (MMP2, complement C1QA, immunoglobulins, GFAP, hemoglobin — all abundant blood proteins) reflect blood contamination rather than BBB breakdown. I could not confirm the dataset identifier or that it contains those identifications. If the attribution is wrong, the central interpretation loses its only external support. The authors should confirm the identifier and the specific claim.

Ref 32 (Gaither 2025) appears mismatched to the claim it supports. The text states "increased BIP levels were found to be positively correlated with alcohol consumption grade and reflected the degree of alcohol-induced damage in human liver biopsy samples 32," but the cited paper's title concerns the ensemble of drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters in human liver. Nothing in the title or metadata indicates it reports BIP/GRP78 correlation with consumption grade. Either the claim or the citation is wrong; the authors should confirm which.

The central claim — that Dep-specific proteins indicate BBB breakdown and neuroinflammation — is not distinguished from the contamination alternative by the evidence presented, and the only citation-based rebuttal is the unverifiable Lourbopoulos claim above. The design aspects (sample-purity controls, blood-marker quantitation) belong to the methods reviewer; from the citation record alone, the rebuttal is a single unverified source.

questions: Confirm that ProteomeXchange dataset PXD053568 (Lourbopoulos 2025) contains the Hb and keratin identifications claimed, and that the identifier is correct.

Confirm that Gaither 2025 (ref 32) actually reports BIP/GRP78 levels correlating with alcohol consumption grade in human liver biopsies; the cited title concerns drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters.
Is the Hashimoto 2025 bioRxiv preprint the correct and current source for the astrocyte immune-activation claim, and does a published version exist?
